results.title: Verda raises prices again — all nine GPUs up about 1%, the eighth rise since Oct 23 | GPUJournal
highlights:
Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 2, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 1: every GPU in Verda's range rose by about 1% — GB300, B300, B200, H200, H100, both A100s, the RTX PRO 6000 and the L40S. After two flat checks, the October rise run has resumed.

Image: Verda via verda.com

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 2, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.05 → $13.18 [$13.18], B300 $11.35 → $11.46 [$11.46], B200 $8.87 → $8.96 [$8.958], H200 $6.25 → $6.31 [$6.313], H100 SXM $4.79 → $4.84 [$4.841], A100 80GB $2.25 → $2.27 [$2.270], A100 40GB $1.61 → $1.63 [$1.625], RTX PRO 6000 $2.65 → $2.67 [$2.671] and L40S $1.90 → $1.92 [$1.920]. Each move is within a cent of +1.0% — a uniform list adjustment, not one card repricing.

...

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $65 per B200 and $35 per H100 on a 730-hour month — small per hour, real per fleet.

Checked today and unchanged: RunPod Secure, Lambda, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute and TensorDock all held at the rates read on Nov 1, and SaladCloud's new Priority rates (RTX 5090 High $0.60, RTX 4090 High $0.44) are still the live ones. Not checked today, and named rather than covered by the stamp: RunPod Community (its tier could not be separated in today's read), Hyperstack (its pricing table could not be read) and nafnaf.ai (its homepage showed no GPUs available today, so there was no live listing to verify).

results.title: GPU Rental Prices 2025-2026: How Fast They Move | Opengrid
highlights:
| When | What happened | Move | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 Jun 2025 | AWS cuts its H100 on-demand price in a single announcement | −44% | AWS, via CloudZero and IntuitionLabs |
| Jun to Jul 2025 | Other providers follow with their own cuts, in single moves | −20% to −25% | CloudZero, IntuitionLabs |
| Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contract price climbs from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour | about +40% | SemiAnalysis |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | Silicon Data H100 rental index rises from $2.00 to $2.20 in four weeks | +10% | Silicon Data |
| 2026 | On-demand capacity sold out across all GPU types | n/a | SemiAnalysis |

...

## Mid-2025: the price war

On 5 June 2025, AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement. That is not a gradual drift. It is nearly half the price, overnight, from the largest cloud provider in the world.

Other providers did not wait long. Through June and July 2025, several cut their own prices by 20% to 25%, again in single moves rather than small steps.

For buyers, this was the moment to renegotiate or move. Teams that had signed earlier contracts, or picked a provider and stayed put, kept paying the old price.

## Late 2025 into 2026: the reversal

Then the direction flipped.

- Contract prices rose about 40%. SemiAnalysis tracked one-year H100 contracts rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026.
- The rental index jumped 10% in four weeks. Silicon Data's H100 rental index went from $2.00 to $2.20 between December 2025 and January 2026.
- Capacity dried up. SemiAnalysis reported on-demand sold out across all GPU types in 2026, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027.

The teams that locked in contracts at the low point did well. The teams that waited paid 40% more for the same commitment a few months later.

## Each GPU moves on its own

It is tempting to think of "GPU prices" as one number. They are not. During the same stretch where the H100 rental index rose 10%, A100 and B200 prices stayed flat (Silicon Data).

Every GPU type has its own price band, and the bands are wide. Thunder Compute's September 2026 data:

| GPU | Price range, $ per hour |
| --- | --- |
| A100 | $1.09 to $5.07 |
| H100 | $2.89 to $11.06 |
| H200 | $3.44 to $10.60 |
| B200 | $3.50 to $27.04 |

Source: Thunder Compute, Sep 2026.

So "is now a good time to rent?" has no single answer. It depends on the chip, the provider and the pricing tier. For a provider-by-provider breakdown, see H100 price per hour in 2026.

results.title: The Cheapest GPU Rental Right Now (November 2026): What 'Cheapest' Actually Means for H100, H200, and B200
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
The takeaway

- Entering November 2026, the cheapest GPU rental depends entirely on which 'cheapest' you mean: the marketplace/spot floor, a reliable named on-demand rate, or the market median — and they can differ by 2–4x on the same card.
- Cheapest reliable on-demand right now: H100 (80GB) ~$1.99–2.89/GPU-hr (Voltage Park ~$1.99, Thunder Compute ~$2.19, RunPod ~$2.89), H200 (141GB) ~$3.59–4.29 (RunPod ~$3.59, Crusoe ~$4.29), B200 (Blackwell) ~$5.50–6.99 (Lambda is the cheapest reliable on-demand B200).
- Marketplace/spot floors go lower and less certain: H100 asks from ~$1.74 (Vast.ai) and spot ~$1.03 (Spheron), H200 asks from ~$2.25–2.76, B200 single-provider floors as low as ~$3.69 but with availability and trust caveats.
- Market medians are much higher: ~$4.20 H100, ~$5.70 H200, ~$8.19 B200 (Uvik's October index) — so a random provider costs roughly double the floor.
- Hyperscalers (AWS/Azure/GCP) stay ~$7–14/hr for the identical card — you pay 3–6x for the platform, not the silicon.
- The real cheapest option is often NOT renting: below ~40–50% duty cycle a per-token API beats renting metal at any of these rates, because a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it works or not.
- And the direction of travel just changed: with Microsoft and Google pausing capex and chip delays pushing capacity to H1 2027, the price floor that stopped falling in October is now firming — the cheapest rate you see today may be the cheapest you'll see for a while.

...

**The cheapest reliable on-demand rate right now (November 2026):**

- H100 (80GB) → ~$1.99–2.89/GPU-hr. Voltage Park ~$1.99, Thunder Compute ~$2.19, RunPod ~$2.89.
- H200 (141GB) → ~$3.59–4.29/hr. RunPod ~$3.59, Crusoe ~$4.29.
- B200 (Blackwell) → ~$5.50–6.99/hr. Lambda is typically the cheapest reliable on-demand Blackwell.

...

Every figure here is a published rate gathered at the end of October 2026 from public pricing pages and multi-provider trackers (getdeploying, Ornn, Uvik, Singularity, Spheron). They move weekly with supply, region, and commitment — read them for the shape, then confirm on the provider's own page before you commit a dollar.

There is no single cheapest GPU cloud: the cheapest provider changes with the GPU, and spot or marketplace offers undercut every on-demand price. Here is the ranking per GPU, with the catches.

Last updated: November 13, 2026 · 9 min read

Quick answer

What is the cheapest GPU cloud for AI right now?

GPUwithCrypto's price check of 29 October 2026 found no single lowest-priced GPU cloud: Massed Compute led on demand for the H100 ($2.73), H200, B200 and L40S, Thunder Compute for the A100 80GB ($1.09), Salad for the RTX 4090 ($0.33). GPUwithCrypto rents each GPU at least 15% below such a reference, in crypto.

In brief

- H100: Massed Compute at $2.73 per GPU-hour on demand; GPUwithCrypto at $2.32/hour.
- A100 80GB: Thunder Compute at $1.09, the lowest 80 GB on-demand rate; GPUwithCrypto at $0.92/hour.
- RTX 4090: Salad at $0.33 on 29 October, $0.44 since 1 November; GPUwithCrypto at $0.28/hour.
- Spot and marketplace: under GPUwithCrypto for all seven GPUs, down to $0.13 for an RTX 4090 on Vast.ai, but interruptible or run by a host.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Index, November 2026: H100 to B300
highlights:
- November 4, 2026
- 7 min read
- By the CoreGPU team

Every month we check the public on-demand prices of specialist GPU clouds to set our own: CoreGPU prices every GPU at least 25% below the market median. This is the data behind that number, as listed on November 4, 2026.

## Method

- One on-demand price per provider and GPU, taken from public pricing pages or price APIs. Prices for 8-GPU nodes are divided by eight.
- Specialist GPU clouds only for the median. Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) are listed separately because their prices are 2.5 to 4.5 times higher.
- Monthly cost = hourly price × 730 hours. Prices exclude taxes.

## Median prices by GPU

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B300 | 8 | 6.60 | 8.98 | $6,552 |
| NVIDIA B200 | 11 | 5.43 | 8.19 | $5,979 |
| NVIDIA H200 | 12 | 2.90 | 4.94 | $3,606 |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | 16 | 1.99 | 3.72 | $2,716 |
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 | 9 | 1.40 | 2.19 | $1,599 |
| NVIDIA L40S | 11 | 0.73 | 1.57 | $1,146 |
| AMD MI325X | 2 | 3.80 | 4.21 | $3,071 |
| AMD MI300X | 4 | 2.59 | 3.22 | $2,351 |

...

On-demand prices per GPU-hour at the largest clouds remain far above specialist clouds: H100 from $6.88 (8-GPU instance divided by eight) to more than $12 depending on the provider, and B300 from $15 to $17.80. Commitments of one to three years cut those prices by 30 to 56%.

## What moved in 2026

- Prices are rising again for flagships. At least one large specialist cloud announced increases of 10 to 26% on H100, H200 and B300 from December 1.
- Clusters cost more than single instances. Multi-node offers are commonly 20 to 50% more per GPU than on-demand single servers.
- Listed is not available. Several providers list GPUs with no deployable region, or “contact sales” for every flagship.
- Fees moved to storage and idle time. Egress is mostly free; stopped-instance storage, public IPs and minimum billing periods are where extra cost appears.

highlights:
Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16 | GPUJournal

# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

results.title: Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23 | S&P Global
highlights:
Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23 | S&P Global 

 November 05, 2026

# Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23

Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, will launch US GPU Compute prices, effective Nov. 23, 2026.

Daily on-demand and interruptible prices will cover four NVIDIA chips: the NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and B300 chips. Prices will be published in US dollars per GPU-hour and US dollars per million tokens of output, based on prices and availability at 1:30 pm CT.

COVERAGE

The assessments reflect the market value of available NVIDIA GPU compute capacity delivered through qualifying virtualized infrastructure services in the US by providers and marketplaces. The new assessments will capture an evolving segment of the compute market, where growing availability of dedicated GPU capacity and increasingly standardized service offerings have supported greater price transparency. The assessments will provide standardized price references for accessing GPU compute capacity in the US, adding further granularity to Platts coverage of the infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence workloads.

METHODOLOGY

Each GPU price will be a simple average of the prices of available GPUs for each chip and service type. Platts will review the prices for outliers and will automatically exclude any prices greater than 2 median absolute deviations from the median.

Platts may review the suitability of the current methodology and consider adopting a volume-weighted average approach once sufficient trade data has been collected. Platts encourages market participants to report trade data to ComputePricing@spglobal.com (PriceGroup@spglobal.com) for this purpose.

### 13 How much does it cost to buy an H200 server?

An eight-GPU HGX H200 server cost $320,000 to $420,000 in July 2026 according to Mercatus, which gives $370,000 as the typical integrated price, while Thunder Compute gives $350,000 to $450,000 and Ace Computers lists a Matrix HGX H200 from $478,992; the SXM module alone sells for $32,000 to $40,000 but needs an HGX baseboard 40 41 42. Add colocation, power for a system that draws about 10 kW at the wall, support and the cost of the money. Under our assumptions, $370,000 of hardware, 40 percent resale after two years, $1,500 a month of colocation, 8 percent cost of capital, $500 a month of support and power at the US commercial average of 13.97 cents per kWh, owning costs about $13,717 a month plus $1.42 per hour of use 43. That never beats GPUBank's on-demand node at $19.92 an hour within a 730-hour month, and it beats the market median only above about 360 hours 4 6. Buying makes sense mainly for teams that would otherwise pay large-cloud rates or must keep data on their own hardware.
